candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hazardous-drug PPE / protective gown selection
candidate.educational_objective: Select appropriate hazardous-drug protective gowns: use a disposable, nonabsorbent barrier garment with long sleeves and tight cuffs, and do not reuse contaminated or previously worn gowns.

options.A: A disposable protective gown made of a nonabsorbent barrier material, with long sleeves and tight-fitting cuffs
options.B: A cloth laboratory coat because absorbent fabric is preferred for hazardous-drug splashes
options.C: A standard short-sleeved isolation garment because chemotherapy gloves alone protect the forearms
options.D: A previously used hazardous-drug gown that is dry and has no visible contamination

candidate.rationale: OSHA hazardous-drug guidance states that protective gowns should not have seams or closures that allow drugs to pass through and should have long sleeves with tight-fitting cuffs. Disposable polyethylene-coated polypropylene or other laminate materials provide better protection than non-coated absorbent materials. Gowns should be disposed of after each use rather than reused. OSHA also notes that there is no single specific performance standard requiring gowns to be labeled 'chemotherapy-tested.' Therefore A is the best answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Hazardous-drug gowns should provide a nonabsorbent protective barrier with long sleeves/tight cuffs and should not be reused; a universal 'chemotherapy-tested gown' designation is not required by a single specific performance standard.
candidate.source_document_title: Hazardous Drugs — Controlling Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Drugs
